item.title: Orlando’s Fall Calendar Goes Well Beyond the Theme Parks
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Orlando’s fall calendar is making the destination relevant to travelers for reasons that extend well beyond its famous theme parks. From the Southern Hill Farms Fall Festival and Winter Park Autumn Art Festival to the Central Florida Veg Fest, EPCOT International Food & Wine Festival and Swan and Dolphin Food & Wine Classic, autumn brings a diverse mix of food, art, seasonal traditions and cultural celebrations. The city’s 94-day Halloween season adds another layer, while events such as FusionFest and Fiesta Calle Orange reflect the many cultures that shape Central Florida.

Music and sports give fall travelers another reason to build a trip around a particular date. Electric Daisy Carnival returns to Tinker Field, the Vans Warped Tour brings punk, alternative and emo music to Camping World Stadium, and concerts by artists including Doja Cat, Olivia Rodrigo and SOMBR add major touring acts to the calendar. Meanwhile, the Orlando Magic, Orlando Solar Bears, Orlando City SC and Orlando Pride offer professional basketball, hockey and soccer. Even the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex joins the culinary calendar with Taste of Space: Fall Bites!, adding a distinctly Central Florida twist to the season.

The Curated Take: Orlando’s fall appeal is increasingly about choosing your own reason to go. A traveler might come for a food festival, an art weekend, a major concert, a soccer match or Halloween, with the city’s broader dining, entertainment and cultural landscape filling in the itinerary. That makes fall less a single Orlando experience and more a collection of distinct ways to experience the destination.

item.title: The Laurel Highlands Makes Fall Foliage a Destination
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Pennsylvania’s Laurel Highlands has earned a place among the country’s standout fall foliage destinations for the seventh consecutive year, placing sixth in the 2026 USA Today 10Best Readers’ Choice Awards for Best Destination for Fall Colors. Set across the Allegheny Mountains, the region typically reaches peak color around mid-October, when its mountain ridges and river valleys take on layers of red, gold, and orange. Nearly 200,000 acres of public lands, along with hiking and biking trails including the Great Allegheny Passage, give visitors plenty of ways to experience the landscape beyond a scenic drive.

The season also brings a distinctly local rhythm to the Laurel Highlands, with festivals and attractions providing reasons to linger. Confluence PumpkinFest, Fort Ligonier Days, Delmont Apple ‘n Arts Festival, and Seven Springs Autumnfest fill the September and October calendar, while the region’s historic sites and architectural landmarks offer another dimension to an autumn visit. Fallingwater, Kentuck Knob, and other Frank Lloyd Wright works, along with Ohiopyle State Park and the area’s mountain resorts, make the foliage backdrop part of a broader cultural and outdoor itinerary.

The Curated Take: The Laurel Highlands is most interesting in fall when the foliage becomes a gateway rather than the entire experience. The combination of mountain landscapes, Frank Lloyd Wright architecture, historic sites, local festivals, craft beverages, and outdoor recreation gives visitors reasons to build an itinerary around the season rather than simply pass through in search of peak color.

item.title: Rethinking What It Means to Age Well in the Texas Hill Country
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Lake Austin Spa Resort is bringing together women working across wellness, healthcare and spa leadership for Better with Age: Women Redefining Longevity, Leadership & Wellbeing on October 14 and 15. Created in partnership with Glowing Older and hosted by its founder, Nancy Griffin, the gathering will explore longevity, women’s health, purpose and wellbeing as part of Lake Austin’s monthlong A Gathering of W.I.S.E. Women series. Speakers include wellness executive Laura Gamboa, Northwestern University professor Dr. Ruchi Gupta and author Susan Salenger, alongside an interactive session focused on personal values.

The program reflects a broader shift in how wellness is approaching aging, moving beyond appearance and conventional anti-aging narratives toward health, purpose, connection and quality of life. Day guests will also have access to Lake Austin’s all-inclusive resort experience, including lunch, spa treatments, wellness programming and lake activities, creating space to consider those ideas within a broader retreat setting.

The Curated Take: The most compelling aspect of Better with Age is its premise that aging well is not simply a matter of extending life, but of considering how we want to live it. Bringing conversations about women’s health, leadership, personal values and longevity into a destination wellness setting makes the retreat part of a larger cultural conversation about what wellbeing looks like across different stages of life.

item.title: Tualatin Valley Finds New Flavors for Fall
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Just 20 minutes from Portland, Oregon, Tualatin Valley offers a gateway into the northern reaches of Willamette Valley wine country, where vineyards and farms increasingly intersect with an ambitious culinary scene. This fall brings several new ways to experience that connection, including Sazanami, a 14-seat, adults-only omakase restaurant from James Beard Award-winning chef Hajime Sato. Opened in July, the nine-course experience changes with the day’s freshest ingredients and emphasizes sustainably sourced seafood, giving Beaverton an intimate destination for serious sushi without a trip into downtown Portland.

The season also brings new ways to experience Oregon’s agricultural bounty. At Ponzi Vineyards, The Laurelwood Table pairs a four-course lunch from chef Eric Ekberg with the estate’s single-vineyard wines, while the Women’s Adventure Weekend Harvest Weekend in October brings together wine, hazelnuts, saké, chocolate making and peak-season produce through a hands-on three-day retreat. Together, the additions highlight a side of the Willamette Valley that is as much about meeting the people, producers and chefs behind the region’s food as it is about tasting the finished product.

The Curated Take: Tualatin Valley’s appeal is increasingly found in the space between city and wine country. Its proximity to Portland makes it easy to reach, but the combination of estate vineyards, agricultural producers and destination-worthy dining gives travelers reasons to slow down and explore beyond the usual Willamette Valley itinerary.

item.title: When Soccer Fandom Becomes a Reason to Travel
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
For millions of soccer fans, following a club is about far more than the 90 minutes on the pitch. New research commissioned by G Adventures for the launch of its Away Games small-group sports travel series suggests that soccer fandom can shape identity, friendships and even travel decisions, with nearly 70 percent of respondents saying the sport gives them a sense of belonging and makes them feel less lonely. Three-quarters have made friends with strangers through soccer, while 64 percent say they would travel with a group of people they had never met if they supported the same club.

That sense of community is increasingly extending beyond home stadiums. The research found that 69 percent of fans said the 2026 World Cup increased their desire to travel internationally for soccer, but overseas match trips can come with their own anxieties. Fake tickets, language barriers, unfamiliar transit systems and the possibility of ending up among rival supporters all ranked among fans’ concerns. Away Games is designed around those friction points, combining guaranteed premium or VIP match tickets with small-group itineraries led by locally based, soccer-focused Chief Experience Officers.

The new trips span some of Europe’s great soccer cities, including Madrid, London, Barcelona and Manchester. Experiences pair major club matches with the culture surrounding them, from local supporter pubs and lower-league terrace matches to tapas tours, food markets, neighborhood explorations and city history. The lineup includes itineraries centered on Real Madrid, Arsenal, Chelsea, FC Barcelona, Manchester City and Manchester United, creating a way for travelers to experience both the spectacle of elite soccer and the communities that surround it.

The Curated Take: The most interesting element of Away Games is the decision to treat soccer as a gateway into a city rather than the sole purpose of the trip. The stadium may be the anchor, but the stronger travel experience is in understanding what a club means to its supporters, where they gather, what they eat and how the sport fits into local identity. For travelers who already see soccer as part of their cultural world, this approach turns fandom into a distinctly social form of travel.

item.title: Bora Bora’s Next Chapter Takes Shape Overwater
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Bora Bora is preparing for a new chapter in luxury hospitality as the former InterContinental Bora Bora Resort & Thalasso Spa undergoes an extensive transformation ahead of its late 2027 reopening as Regent Bora Bora. The new resort will mark Regent Hotels & Resorts’ debut in French Polynesia, bringing the brand to a private motu on the eastern edge of Bora Bora’s lagoon.

The 84-villa resort will be exclusively overwater, with direct lagoon access and views toward Mount Otemanu and the open Pacific. The renovation will introduce Regent’s approach to contemporary luxury while retaining the natural and cultural character of the setting, with immersive dining, personalized service and experiences designed to connect guests with Polynesian culture. Regent’s signature Personal Havens and Regent Experience Agents will also become part of the guest experience.

The resort’s sustainability story will continue as well. Its existing seawater air-conditioning system draws naturally cold water from the depths of the Pacific to cool the property, reducing the electricity required for air conditioning and refrigeration by approximately 90 percent. The system will remain in operation following the transformation, preserving an unusual piece of environmental innovation as the resort enters its next era.

The Curated Take: The most interesting aspect of Regent Bora Bora is not simply the arrival of another luxury brand in an iconic destination. It is the opportunity to see an established resort reimagined without losing the qualities that make its setting distinctive. An exclusively overwater design, Polynesian cultural connection and an existing sustainability innovation give the transformation a story that goes beyond a brand conversion.

item.title: Art Deco in the Outback
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
There is a striking visual dissonance that occurs when you look through a frame of polished timber and brushed brass onto three hundred miles of unvarnished red dirt. Inside the carriage, the lines are clean, curved, and disciplined—the geometry of Art Deco, quieted by the tactile warmth of saddle leather, decorative timber, and fine sheepskin. Outside, the landscape is sprawling, wind-scoured, and indifferent to human geometry.

To the untrained eye, Art Deco and the Australian Outback might seem like awkward bedfellows: an urban, European design movement dropped into the silica dust of the Red Center. But in Australia, these two forces share an intimate, historical alliance. Understanding that relationship is the secret to understanding why long-distance rail travel across this continent remains one of the world’s most evocative cultural passages.

The Interwar Frontier: Modernism in Red Dirt

In the 1920s and 1930s, Australia was experiencing an extraordinary industrial and pastoral boom. Wealth flowed directly out of the ground—driven by wool clip, wheat harvests, cattle drives, and rich veins of gold. As transcontinental rail tracks were laid to stitch isolated inland settlements to coastal ports, a distinct architectural wave followed the iron rails inward.

When Art Deco arrived from Paris and Hollywood, remote frontier towns embraced it with fierce pride. Streamlined, curve-cornered pubs, civic halls, and railway stations built from rendered brick, vitrolite glass, and terrazzo sprang up in dusty mining and pastoral outposts like Kalgoorlie and Broken Hill. These structures were more than shelter; they were bold monuments to modern ambition—physical declarations that culture, elegance, and connectivity had arrived on the edge of the wilderness.

Tactile Storytelling Onboard

That historical interwar spirit finds its modern rebirth aboard Journey Beyond’s Aurora Australis Suites aboard the Indian Pacific and The Ghan. Designed by Woods Bagot, the carriages deliberately step away from generic modern minimalism to embrace an artisanal, heritage-driven palette.

The materials chosen for the interiors—smooth timber veneers, sculpted stone surfaces, tactile sheepskin, and rich leather—are direct nods to the pastoral commodities that built the nation’s interior economy. These are the textures of the drovers, wool merchants, and railway builders who shaped Australia’s early cross-continental trade.

“The luxury interiors are characterised by an artisanal, heritage-driven approach to detail and meticulous craftsmanship. Featuring a palette of decorative timber, stone surfaces, and accents of sheepskin and leather, the interiors create a rich and layered experience that reflects both heritage and landscape.”

— Rosina Di Maria, Director at Woods Bagot

Paired with private butler service, curated regional dining featuring Kangaroo Island lobster and premium Wagyu, and Champagne Bollinger served in crystal glass, the suite becomes a living capsule. It honors the interwar golden age of rail travel without feeling like a museum piece.

Overlapping Timelines: From Gold Mines to Sacred Waterholes

As the train cuts its steady path across the continent, the real power of the journey reveals itself in the layer cake of history visible outside the window. The rail line acts as a moving corridor connecting three distinct temporal scales:

1. Modern Pastoral & Industrial Heritage: At Kalgoorlie in Western Australia, passengers step off into the legacy of Paddy Hannan’s 1893 gold rush, exploring historic sites before soaring over the vast pit of the mining frontier. In the Adelaide Hills, the train pauses near stone winemaking estates established during the same interwar period.

2. Deep Geological Time & First Nations Memory: When The Ghan pauses at Katherine or Alice Springs, guests take to the sky by helicopter or plane to reach Nitmiluk Gorge and Uluru. Here, the polished lines of the train yield to 13 deep sandstone gorges carved by ancient rivers and sacred monoliths carrying tens of thousands of years of First Nations songlines and rock art around Mutitjulu Waterhole.

3. The Cadence of the Present: Inside the carriage, travelers observe both timelines passing in slow motion—paying the price of distance in time rather than flying blind over the continent’s immense heart.

The Story Continues

Rail travel remains unmatched in its ability to tell complex stories of place. By marrying the geometric elegance of Art Deco craftsmanship with the unyielding majesty of the outback, journeys like The Ghan and the Indian Pacific do not merely carry passengers across geography. They transport them through overlapping eras—proving that on the rails, the story of Australian heritage continues to unfold with every passing mile.

This piece is part of the latest issue of Curated Travel Magazine, where we explore travel through immersive stories, cultural insight, and thoughtfully curated experiences around the world.

item.title: The Algarve After Summer
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Autumn brings a different rhythm to Portugal’s Algarve, where warm days, golden coastlines and fewer crowds make the season particularly appealing for a coastal escape. At W Algarve in Albufeira, the change of season is an invitation to spend more time outdoors, from exploring the region’s dramatic cliffs to getting out on the water.

The hotel’s Whatever/Whenever service can arrange experiences that take advantage of the landscape, including coasteering and cliff jumping, private kayak excursions into the Benagil caves, and surfing lessons along the Algarve coast. Closer to the hotel, Evaristo and Castelo beaches offer a quieter way to experience the shoreline, with scenic cliff walks and broad views over the Atlantic. Back at the resort, newly added padel, pickleball and tennis courts bring another dimension to an active autumn stay.

The Curated Take: The Algarve is at its most interesting when the intensity of summer begins to ease. Autumn makes room for a more leisurely relationship with the coast, whether that means exploring its caves and cliffs, walking between beaches or lingering outdoors without the pressure of peak-season crowds. W Algarve provides a contemporary base for experiencing that quieter side of southern Portugal.

item.title: A Taste of Spain Above Bangkok
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Three years after opening in Bangkok’s On Nut neighborhood, INNSiDE by Meliá Bangkok Sukhumvit is marking the occasion by leaning into one of its most distinctive features: the skyline. Rising 34 floors above the city, the 208-room hotel combines contemporary design with a distinctly Spanish influence, culminating in LUZ Bangkok Tapas Bar on the 33rd floor and a transparent infinity pool directly overhead.

The hotel’s “Feel the Skyline Vibes” experience brings that combination together through Spanish tapas, cocktails and a sunset cocktail-making class overlooking Bangkok. At LUZ, guests can sample tapas, Spanish wines, cocktails and signature sangrias under the direction of Spanish Chef de Cuisine Juan Ignacio García Racionero, known as Chef Nacho. The restaurant’s position beneath the transparent pool creates one of the property’s more unusual visual moments, while the 34th-floor pool provides another perspective on the city. The hotel also incorporates co-working spaces, giving the property a distinctly contemporary take on the urban hotel.

The Curated Take: LUZ gives INNSiDE Bangkok a particularly interesting identity. Rather than simply adding a rooftop bar to a city hotel, the property has created a vertical experience where Spanish food and hospitality meet Bangkok’s skyline. It is a reminder that a sense of place in a city hotel doesn’t necessarily mean reproducing the destination literally. Sometimes it comes from the unexpected conversation between two cultures.

item.title: Las Ventanas al Paraíso Captures the Soul of Southern Baja
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Las Ventanas al Paraíso, A Rosewood Resort has earned a place among the world’s leading hotels, ranking No. 25 on The 50 Best Hotels 2026 list. The Los Cabos resort also received the WhistlePig Highest Climber Award after moving up 19 places from its No. 44 position in 2025, marking its second consecutive year on the global ranking.

Set along the coast of Southern Baja, Las Ventanas is designed around the meeting of desert and sea, with Mexican artistry and regional craftsmanship woven throughout its 84 suites and villas. Five restaurants and bars draw on the produce and flavors of the region, while the resort’s experiences range from horseback riding along the beach and healing rituals at its spa to sunrise yoga and time spent beside its eight pools. The property also offers 30 Rosewood Residences, including the distinctive Ty Warner Mansion.

The 2026 ranking was compiled from votes by more than 800 members of The 50 Best Hotels Academy, comprising hoteliers, travel journalists, educators and experienced luxury travelers. For Las Ventanas, the recognition reinforces a hospitality philosophy centered not simply on luxury, but on creating a strong connection to the landscape, culture and craftsmanship of Southern Baja.

The Curated Take: Las Ventanas works because its luxury is deeply tied to where it is. The resort doesn’t need to manufacture a sense of place when the contrast between the Baja desert and the Sea of Cortez is already so distinctive. Mexican art, local craftsmanship, regional cuisine and experiences rooted in the landscape give the property an identity that extends well beyond its accommodations.
